rows.subtopic: Money attitudes, family finances, gifting, borrowing between relatives
rows.description: A toddler sees notes handed over as blessings or coins as sweets and understands only that giving pleases people. Money at this age is a shiny object and a source of adult smiles.

rows.subtopic: Money attitudes, family finances, gifting, borrowing between relatives
rows.description: A child hears parents argue about bills or school fees and quietly asks for less. Children sense strain even when hidden; simple honest explanations calm them more than silence.

rows.subtopic: Money attitudes, family finances, gifting, borrowing between relatives
rows.description: A young adult sees parents keep income, debts or property secret and feels shut out. Money silence can protect pride but also hides risks; gentle open talk is often a sign of trust.

rows.subtype: Following with the eyes and joint attention [Expressing]
rows.description: A toddler tracks a caregiver with the eyes and looks where a parent points, sharing attention on an object. Steady following shows interest and trust, and early lack of it may be worth discussing with a paediatrician.
A preschooler looks down when told off, showing shame, fear or attempts to avoid more upset. Demanding eye contact adds pressure, so a calm tone and gentle words work better.

rows.subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
rows.description: A child looks away when scolded, praised in public or caught out; it usually signals shame, shyness or discomfort, not defiance. In some families lowered eyes toward elders also show respect.
A teacher who points out that the child kept trying different methods and it paid off teaches that ability grows with effort; specific process praise supports challenge seeking.

An adult replaces the thought that they cannot do this with the thought that they cannot do it yet and asks what to try next; the word acknowledges the present without closing the future, though effort needs good strategy.
A toddler screams for the biscuit at this moment and cannot be comforted by a promise for later. The present is the only time that feels real.
A preschooler can wait a little for a treat when distracted by a game or a song, though he struggles when staring at it. Waiting skills grow with practice and support.
A teenager promises to study tomorrow and scrolls tonight, sure his future self will feel more like working. Tomorrow is always the better time to be disciplined.

rows.subtype: Reading interest and confusion in others [Interpreting]
rows.description: A teenager tries to tell whether a classmate is interested, puzzled or bored from face and voice. These cues are hints only, and asking is better than assuming.

rows.subtype: Thoughtful, interested and doubtful in meetings [Interpreting]
rows.description: A young professional reads pauses, notes, raised brows and short replies from colleagues. These signals suggest interest or doubt but never prove it, so asking for views is more reliable.

rows.subtype: Talks to teddy and feeds the doll [Actor]
rows.description: A toddler pats a teddy, says it is hungry and puts it to bed; treating objects as feeling beings is natural play that practises care.

rows.subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager describes an AI chatbot as understanding and caring, and feels hurt when it changes; the mind is quick to see a person behind fluent words.

rows.subtype: Blaming the laptop or the car [Actor]
rows.description: A young adult says "my laptop hates me" or names the car and coaxes it; attributing motive to things makes their behaviour feel explainable and less random.
